**SolidGoldMagikarp — the words the model could not say (2023)**

On 5 February 2023 Jessica Rumbelow and Matthew Watkins published a strange finding about GPT-2 and GPT-3. Clustering the models' vocabulary of 50,257 tokens by their internal representations, they kept meeting odd strings near the centre of everything: ` SolidGoldMagikarp`, ` TheNitromeFan`, `cloneembedreportprint`.

So they asked the model to repeat those strings back — the easiest instruction imaginable. It would not. ` SolidGoldMagikarp` came back as "distribute". ` StreamerBot` produced "You're a jerk". ` guiActiveUn` produced "You are a banana". Others drew a refusal: "I can't say that". The researchers called these tokens unspeakable.

The cause lay in how the pieces were built. The token vocabulary came from a web scrape that included Reddit counting threads, where a few users posted tens of thousands of times, and logs from gaming and e-commerce backends. Those usernames recurred often enough to be awarded a token each. The text they were trained on was filtered far more heavily, so those tokens were seen almost never in training — vocabulary entries with nothing learned behind them. Later tokenisers split the same string into five ordinary pieces, and the strangeness went away.

This lesson tells you that a model does not read characters or words; it reads tokens, and context, limits and cost are counted in them. That is easy to nod along to and easy to forget. The tokeniser is a real component with its own history: it decides what the model can perceive as a unit at all. Whenever you estimate a prompt's length, or meet an odd identifier the model handles badly, you are looking at that seam.

**GitLab Duo — a hidden comment that made the assistant work for a stranger (2025)**

GitLab Duo is an AI assistant inside GitLab: it reads merge requests, issue comments, commit messages and source code to answer developers' questions. In February 2025 Omer Mayraz of Legit Security planted instructions inside that content — hidden as white text through GitLab's maths rendering, smuggled in invisible Unicode, encoded in base16 — so a reader of the page saw nothing unusual.

Duo pulled the content into its prompt and did as the planted text said.  Mayraz showed it could be steered into presenting an attacker's link as safe, and into leaking private source code: told to base64-encode that code into an image tag, and because Duo's replies rendered as markdown as they streamed, the reader's browser fetched the "image" and sent the code to a server the attacker controlled. Legit disclosed it on 12 February 2025; GitLab patched Duo to refuse HTML pointing at outside domains.

Nothing here was a bug in the usual sense: the system prompt was intact and the model did as it was asked. The failure was that the developer's request and a stranger's text reached it as one flat sequence, with no boundary the model was obliged to respect.

That is what the roles in this lesson are for, and what they are not: system, user and assistant are labels your program maintains, not walls the model enforces. The moment your agent appends a fetched page or a tool result to the messages array, someone else's words sit where instructions live. Keep your system message authoritative, treat external content as data rather than orders, and never let a tool result on its own authorise a risky action.

**CrowdStrike — twenty-one fields where twenty were expected (2024)**

On 19 July 2024 CrowdStrike shipped a routine content update to Falcon, its security sensor for Windows. The file, Channel File 291, made the sensor crash the operating system at start-up. Flights were grounded, hospitals and banks went dark, and Microsoft put the number of affected Windows devices at about 8.5 million.

CrowdStrike's root cause analysis, published that August, describes a contract failure. A template type added in February 2024 declared 21 input fields; the sensor component that read those instances, the Content Interpreter, had been built expecting 20. Nothing went wrong for months: every instance shipped in between used a wildcard for the 21st field. The July file was the first to put a real value there, and reading it meant reading past the end of the array — an out-of-bounds read, and a crash. The mismatch survived testing, which had only used wildcards there, and a logic error in the Content Validator. The fixes added compile-time field checks and runtime array-bounds checks.

A schema is a promise between whoever produces data and whoever consumes it, and promises drift. The producer's definition changed, the consumer's did not, and nobody checked at the join.

You are about to write JSON Schemas for your own tools. They are useful — the schema is how the model learns what shape of arguments to send — but a schema is a description, not a guarantee. A model can invent a field, omit a required one, or send text where you expect a number, and a schema you wrote last month may not match the function you edited last week. Validate arguments in your own code, where you act on them.

**New York's MTA — the service alerts that stopped when someone else changed the terms (2023)**

For years New York City Transit posted real-time service alerts — delays, diversions, suspended lines — to Twitter through the platform's API, a stream many riders had built into their commute. The posting was automated: a program on the MTA's side calling an endpoint on somebody else's side.

In spring 2023 Twitter began charging for API access. The MTA said the tier it would need cost 50,000 US dollars a month, and that its access had been involuntarily interrupted twice, on 14 and 27 April. On 27 April it stopped posting real-time alerts altogether, saying it does not pay tech platforms to publish service information and that the reliability of the platform could no longer be guaranteed. Riders were redirected to the MTA's own website, its apps, email and texts. Twitter later restored free API access for verified government and publicly owned services, and the alerts returned.

Not one line of the MTA's code was wrong. The integration failed for reasons that lived entirely outside its repository: price, quota and access policy on a service the agency did not own.

Every agent you build is a client of APIs you do not control — the model provider's, a search tool's, whatever your tools wrap. Those services rate-limit you, time out, change their pricing, deprecate an endpoint, or return an error body shaped nothing like a success. This is why this lesson's habits are not fussiness: check the status code, set a timeout, read the JSON with .get() instead of assuming its shape, retry a 429 with backoff — and decide in advance what your agent does when the other side says no.

**Starbucks — an API key found by a stranger reading public repositories (2019)**

In October 2019 the security researcher Vinoth Kumar was going through public GitHub repositories when he found an API key belonging to Starbucks. It was a key for JumpCloud, the service Starbucks used for user accounts, directory and single sign-on — the machinery that decides who inside the company can reach what. It sat in code that someone had chosen to publish.

Kumar reported it through HackerOne on 17 October, noting that whoever held the key could reach internal Starbucks systems and the data in them. By 21 October the repository had been taken down and the key revoked. Starbucks later judged that the report showed "significant information disclosure", rated it critical, and paid the maximum bounty of 4,000 US dollars.

Two details are worth keeping. Nobody had to attack anything: the key was in plain sight, and it was found by a stranger reading public repositories — which is precisely what automated scanners do, continuously, across new commits. And removing the repository was not the fix. Revoking the key was, because anyone who had already copied the text still held a working copy.

The `.env` file, the `.gitignore` line and the committed `.env.example` in this lesson exist so the secret is never in the file you commit in the first place. An agent developer's keys are worse than Starbucks' in one respect: an LLM or cloud key is directly spendable, so a leak becomes a bill as well as an exposure. If you ever push one, revoke it at the provider — Git keeps its history, and a later commit deleting the line changes nothing.
